questions.prompt: Omar is about to hand a task to Quill. Which of these is the clearest sign that the task is too big for one session?

options.text: The task touches a file in src/ and a file in tests/.
Omar cannot name the files the task will touch, and no single command proves it is done.
The definition of done mentions make test.
The task is a refactor rather than a new feature.

explanations.a: A source file plus its test is the normal shape of a well-sized task. CR-110 touches exactly that and fits in one session.
explanations.b: Correct. A well-sized task has a definition of done, touches a handful of files you can list, and is verified with one command. When you cannot list the files or name the command, size it first: one plan, several sessions.
explanations.c: Naming the verifying command is a sign the task is well-sized, not too big. It is the one command that proves the work is done.
explanations.d: Refactors can be small. CR-111 is too big because it spans a whole module, not because it is a refactor. Step 1 of its plan, one file and its test, is a fine single session.

questions.prompt: In plan mode, what can the agent do and what can it not do?

options.text: It can read and search the repository and propose steps, but it cannot edit files or run commands that change anything.
It can edit files but cannot run tests until the plan is approved.
It can do everything it normally does, but it writes a plan first.
It cannot read files; it plans from the task message alone.

explanations.a: Correct. Plan mode is read-only for the codebase. The agent reads and searches, proposes a plan, and only after you edit and approve does the session leave plan mode and start changing files.
explanations.b: Edits are exactly what plan mode forbids. The point is that nothing is built until you have read and edited the plan.
explanations.c: If the agent could edit while planning, the plan would be a description of work already done. Plan mode holds the edits until you approve.
explanations.d: A plan written without reading the code would be a guess. Quill read src/orders/ before listing the four steps and the files each one touches.

questions.prompt: Quill's third action on step 1 changes the signature of createOrder. Which message is the best steer?

options.text: Three paragraphs explaining the history of the orders module and why the public API matters to the gift card code.
"Please be more careful with this refactor."
"Stop. Do not change the function signatures; only the bodies."
Say nothing now and mention it in the pull request review.

explanations.a: A long explanation goes into the context and competes with the brief. In Omar's failed session, Quill acknowledged three paragraphs and kept changing signatures.
explanations.b: "Careful" is not an instruction. It names no action to stop and no action to take instead, so the agent cannot act on it.
explanations.c: Correct. One sentence, early, naming what to stop and what to do instead. Quill reverted the signature and rewrote only the body.
explanations.d: By review time the wrong signature may have spread to every caller. The cheapest correction is the one made before the wrong edit lands.

questions.prompt: When should Omar restart the session rather than steer it again?

options.text: As soon as the agent makes its first mistake.
When he has corrected the same thing twice and the agent has done it a third time.
Only when the tests are all red.
Never; restarting loses all the work done so far.

explanations.a: A first mistake is what steering is for. One specific sentence usually fixes it. Restarting on every slip throws away good context.
explanations.b: Correct. A correction that has to be repeated has failed; the session has drifted. Restart with the lesson written into the task message or the brief, as Jun did with the callback adapters.
explanations.c: Red tests are one signal, but a session can drift with tests half green. Repeated corrections, growing diffs, and losing track of what changed are the signs.
explanations.d: Committed work survives a restart, and the plan survives because it is a file. What is lost is the drifted context, which is the thing you want to lose.

questions.prompt: Omar runs /compact at turn 30 of a long session. What is the risk?

options.text: The agent loses access to the repository and must re-read every file.
The summary keeps what looks important and may drop a constraint typed early, such as "keep the public API."
The session is closed and a new one starts.
Nothing; compaction is lossless.

explanations.a: Files are still on disk and the agent can read them again. What compaction changes is the conversation history, not the repository.
explanations.b: Correct. Compaction is a summary written by the model. It cannot know that the sentence at turn 3 was the whole point. Put constraints in plan.md, the task message, or CLAUDE.md, where a file is read again instead of summarized away.
explanations.c: That describes /clear. Compaction keeps the session open with a shorter history.
explanations.d: A summary is shorter than the original, so something is always dropped. The compaction in Omar's failed session dropped the signature constraint.

questions.prompt: Why does Omar create a git worktree before running CR-112 in parallel with CR-110?

options.text: So the two sessions can share one set of files and see each other's progress.
Because Claude Code refuses to start a second session in the same folder.
So each session has its own files, its own branch, and its own test runs, and neither sees the other's half-finished edits.
To make make test run faster.

explanations.a: Sharing is the problem, not the goal. Two sessions in one checkout see each other's uncommitted edits and may "fix" them.
explanations.b: There is no such refusal. Two sessions in one checkout will run; they will also race. The worktree is a git safeguard, not an agent rule.
explanations.c: Correct. git worktree add ../shelf-cr112 -b cr-112 gives the second session its own working directory on its own branch. Plain git, no agent flag.
explanations.d: Test speed is unchanged. The worktree exists so that one session's make test does not pick up the other session's broken file.

questions.prompt: Describe a session you would restart rather than steer, and say what you would add to the brief or the task message before restarting.
rubric: Describes a specific session with a repeated or drifting mistake (not a first mistake)
Gives a reason restart beats another correction (drift, repeated correction, growing diff, or lost track of changes)
Names a concrete line to add to the brief, plan.md, or the opening task message
The added line names an action to stop or take, not a request to be careful
questions.modelAnswer: I would restart the CR-111 session where Quill added a callback adapter for compatibility, removed it when told, then added another two edits later, and a third in util.ts. Two corrections had already failed, the diff was growing, and each correction added turns that pushed the original constraint further back in the context. Before restarting I would put one line in the task message: "Do not add callback adapters or compatibility wrappers anywhere. If a caller still passes a callback, stop and tell me which one." That line names the action to stop and the action to take instead. If the same thing happened on a later task, it would earn a line in CLAUDE.md under conventions. The fresh session then starts with the rule in front of it rather than under forty turns of history.

questions.prompt: Split CR-112 (a nightly job that emails each store manager a sales summary) into sessions. For each session give the goal, the files, the done check, and what the next session must not touch.
rubric: Defines at least three sessions, each with one goal
Every session names the files it touches
Every session has a done check that is a command or a test (for example make test green)
Each session states what it must not touch, and src/email/ or migrations/ appears as a boundary at least once
The failing test or the reproduction comes before the implementation in at least one session
Sessions are ordered so that each one starts from the previous one's committed, green state
questions.modelAnswer:
Session 1: the summary query. Goal: a function that returns yesterday's sales per store. Files: src/orders/summary.ts and tests/orders/summary.test.ts. Start with the test, run make test, and see it fail before writing the function. Done: make test green, committed. Must not touch: src/email/, anything under scheduling, migrations/.

Session 2: the email template. Goal: render one manager's summary as an email body. Files: src/email/sales-summary.ts and tests/email/sales-summary.test.ts. This session will ask before editing under src/email/, and Omar answers in this terminal. Done: make test green, the rendered body matches a fixture, committed. Must not touch: src/orders/, the scheduler, and no sending, only rendering.

Session 3: the nightly schedule. Goal: a job that runs at 02:00, calls the summary, renders the email, and hands it to the existing mailer once per manager. Files: src/email/nightly.ts, tests/email/nightly.test.ts. The test asserts one send per manager with the clock mocked. Done: make test green, committed. Must not touch: the summary query, the template, migrations/, and no retry logic.

Session 4: wiring and docs. Goal: register the job at startup and add a line to docs/email.md. Files: src/email/index.ts, docs/email.md. Done: make test green, npm run lint clean, committed. Must not touch: anything in sessions 1 to 3.

Each session opens with /clear and "Read plan.md. Do step N only. Stop when make test is green." If Omar runs session 1 alongside CR-110, he uses git worktree add ../shelf-cr112 -b cr-112 first.
